items.title: Coinbase Adds Fixed-Rate USDC Loans Backed by Bitcoin, Locking In Rate and Maturity at Origination
items.content:
On September 22 local time, U.S. crypto-asset exchange Coinbase added a fixed-rate product for borrowing the dollar stablecoin USDC against Bitcoin collateral. Alongside its existing variable-rate product, users can now choose a loan whose interest rate and repayment date are set when the loan is originated.
The new product uses Morpho's decentralized-finance lending protocol, Morpho Midnight. Coinbase provides the interface for applying for and managing the loan in its app, Morpho supplies the underlying lending infrastructure, and transactions settle on the Base blockchain. Morpho said the outstanding balance of Coinbase's existing variable-rate loans exceeds $1.4 billion and is backed by about $3 billion in collateral.
According to a Coinbase representative quoted by The Block, the available maturities at the time of publication were the last Friday of the current month or the following month. Loan rates are determined by supply and demand between lenders and borrowers. Coinbase's official guidance says the applicable rate and borrowing limit are displayed in the app. A fixed-rate loan must be repaid in full by maturity, and early repayment does not reduce the contracted interest. Failure to repay by maturity may result in liquidation of the collateral, while the collateral may also be liquidated before maturity if its value falls to the liquidation threshold.
items.metanomia_thought: Bitcoin-backed loans allow holders to raise needed funds without selling their Bitcoin. The fixed-rate product adds the ability to calculate interest costs in advance, expanding the options for putting the asset to use while continuing to hold it. The reasons to keep holding Bitcoin therefore extend beyond expectations of price appreciation to its utility as collateral for obtaining funds when needed.

items.title: NYSE and Blockchain.com Pursue Tokenized Stock and ETF Trading Service, Subject to Regulatory Approval
items.content:
On September 23 local time, NYSE Group and crypto-asset services company Blockchain.com announced that they had signed a memorandum of understanding for a tokenized-securities trading service. The plan is to connect Blockchain.com users to a digital alternative trading system under development by NYSE, allowing them to trade tokenized U.S.-listed stocks and exchange-traded funds. The service is contingent on the necessary regulatory approvals.
In January, NYSE announced plans to develop a separate platform for trading tokenized securities and settling transactions on a blockchain. Its proposed features include trading 24 hours a day, seven days a week, instant settlement, orders entered as dollar amounts rather than numbers of shares, and account funding with stablecoins. Holders of tokenized shares would also receive the same dividend and voting rights as holders of conventional shares.
The collaboration also includes an exchange of market data. ICE Data Services, a unit of NYSE parent Intercontinental Exchange, would distribute Blockchain.com's crypto-asset market data and analytics to its clients, while Blockchain.com would integrate selected ICE and NYSE exchange data into its app. Blockchain.com said this would provide real-time stock-price information to its more than 44 million verified accounts.
The announcement concerns a memorandum of understanding covering plans to distribute the trading service; it does not mean that the service has launched. The announcement did not provide a specific launch date, eligible securities, available countries, or a timetable for regulatory approval.
items.metanomia_thought: Expanding a tokenized stock market requires not only a trading system but also investors who will use it. NYSE is seeking access to Blockchain.com's existing customer base, while Blockchain.com is trying to extend customer relationships that began in crypto into U.S. equity investing. The collaboration shows how the customer base built by a crypto platform can become a business asset for traditional exchanges seeking to develop a new market.

items.title: SoFi Begins Settling Its Card Payments in Stablecoins on Mastercard Network; Merchants Need Not Hold Tokens
items.content:
On September 22 local time, U.S. fintech company SoFi announced that it had begun settling debit- and credit-card payments from its subsidiary SoFi Bank using its own stablecoin, SoFiUSD. The settlement applies to transactions on Mastercard's payment network. SoFi described the launch as the first time a U.S. nationally chartered bank has gone live with stablecoin settlement on the Mastercard network.
Settlement is the process in which financial institutions exchange funds after a card payment. Consumers continue using their cards as before, while SoFiUSD is used to settle the funds behind the transaction. The company said merchants neither need to hold the stablecoin nor change their payment systems.
Merchants receive the funds through SoFi's corporate-finance platform, Big Business Banking. SoFi CEO Anthony Noto said merchants using the platform can receive settlement funds immediately in a SoFi Bank account and withdraw them as cash without time restrictions or fees.
SoFiUSD is a crypto asset designed to track the value of the U.S. dollar and is issued by SoFi Bank under the supervision of the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency. The company said each SoFiUSD can be redeemed for one dollar and is backed by reserves composed primarily of cash. However, it is not a bank deposit even though it is issued by a bank. SoFi disclosed that the token is not protected by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation or the Securities Investor Protection Corporation, that the bank does not guarantee its value, and that the value may decline.
The service follows a partnership announced by SoFi and Mastercard in March. SoFi projected that transactions processed in SoFiUSD under the card program would exceed $25 billion on an annualized basis. That figure is a projection, not actual processing volume. The announcement did not disclose the actual volume processed since launch, the blockchain used for settlement, or a timetable for expanding to international transactions.
items.metanomia_thought: SoFi and Mastercard chose to change the instrument used to exchange funds behind the scenes while allowing customers to keep using familiar cards. The case shows that, in stablecoin competition, becoming the settlement instrument for transactions handled by existing banks and payment networks may matter as much as attracting consumers directly—and that financial companies with established transaction networks may lead adoption.

items.title: Canada's Big Six Banks Explore Joint Canadian-Dollar Tokenized Deposit for Transfers Between Financial Institutions
items.content:
On September 22 local time, Canada's six largest banks announced that they are exploring the joint development of a Canadian-dollar-based digital currency, beginning with tokenized deposits. The participating banks are Bank of Montreal, Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, National Bank of Canada, Royal Bank of Canada, Scotiabank, and TD Bank Group.
A tokenized deposit represents a bank deposit in the form of a digital token. In the first stage, the banks will examine how tokenized deposits could be transferred efficiently among Canadian financial institutions. Their longer-term goal is to connect them with other digital-asset initiatives. The concept is intended to increase payment speed and efficiency and support payments executed according to preset conditions while preserving existing safety and regulatory oversight.
The participating banks said they are working together to maintain the competitiveness and security of Canada's payment infrastructure as digital currencies develop globally. They said other deposit-taking institutions are expected to join at an appropriate time.
Canada's central bank, RBC, TD, and other participants completed Project Samara in March. In that trial, a C$100 million bond issued by Export Development Canada was traded on a distributed ledger and settled using central-bank deposits.
The six banks' announcement concerns an exploration of joint development; neither issuance of the tokenized deposit nor launch of a commercial service has been confirmed. The announcement did not identify a specific operator, technical design, timetable, or role for the Bank of Canada.
items.metanomia_thought: If tokenized deposits cannot be exchanged with other financial institutions, their usefulness remains limited. By making inter-institutional transfers the first objective, Canada's six largest banks are exploring how to extend the use of tokenized deposits beyond each bank's own customer base. The significance of the initiative lies in testing whether banks that compete for customers can jointly build the infrastructure through which money moves.

items.title: Binance Invests $100 Million in Circle and Signs Five-Year Agreement to Expand USDC Distribution
items.content:
USDC issuer Circle disclosed in a current report filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on September 22 local time that it had received a $100 million investment from Binance and entered a five-year agreement to expand USDC distribution. The agreement was signed and the investment transaction closed on September 17.
Binance purchased 1,237,011 newly issued shares of Circle's Class A common stock in a private placement at $80.84 per share. It did not buy shares from an existing shareholder; Circle issued new shares to provide capital to the company. According to the filing, the purchase price represented a discount to the market price before closing, but the discount rate was not disclosed.
Under the business agreement, Circle will pay Binance a monthly incentive fee equal to a specified percentage of the amount of USDC held through Circle's Modular Smart Contract Wallet service. Binance will undertake activities to promote USDC use on its platform. The new agreement replaces agreements signed in November 2024 and August 2025. Each party may terminate the agreement before the end of its five-year term if specified events occur. As a general rule, Binance may not sell, transfer, or pledge the acquired shares for two years after closing. Hedging and derivative transactions that transfer the economic risk of share ownership to another party are also restricted. Exceptions apply, including certain transfers among affiliates, and the restriction may end before two years if Binance terminates the business agreement under specified conditions. Shareholder rights, including voting rights, remain in effect during the restricted period.
The filing did not disclose the incentive-fee rate, the USDC balance on which it will be calculated, or the specific events that permit early termination. The public information therefore is insufficient to calculate the amount Binance will receive.
items.metanomia_thought: Binance receives greater compensation as the USDC balance in wallets covered by the agreement increases. Because it now also owns Circle shares, Binance is both helping expand USDC use and investing in the issuer's growth. An exchange's decision to promote a particular stablecoin can therefore be shaped by incentive agreements and equity relationships with the issuer.

items.title: European Central Banks Propose Wider Stablecoin Interest Ban Covering Lending and Staking Rewards
items.content:
On September 22 local time, the European System of Central Banks (ESCB), comprising the European Central Bank and the national central banks of European Union member states, proposed extending the ban on interest paid on stablecoins to rewards delivered through lending and staking. The proposal appeared in its response to the European Commission's consultation on a review of the EU Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA). The response also proposed replacing requirements to hold stablecoin reserves in bank deposits with requirements for short-term liquidity.
MiCA currently prohibits stablecoin issuers and crypto-asset service providers from paying interest to holders. The ESCB said the ban should also apply to crypto-asset lending, borrowing, and staking, which currently fall outside MiCA's scope. This would cover arrangements that combine services or alter the form of rewards while producing an effect equivalent to interest payments. The response said decentralized-finance services could circumvent the ban by turning stablecoins into yield-bearing products through lending, staking, and similar activities.
For reserves, the ESCB proposed eliminating the minimum proportion that must be held as bank deposits and instead requiring issuers to hold specified proportions of assets maturing within one business day and five business days. It said concentrating reserves in bank deposits could allow mass stablecoin redemptions to transmit liquidity pressure to banks because issuers might withdraw deposits all at once to repay customers. The ESCB said the European Banking Authority's draft technical standards could serve as the starting point for the specific liquidity ratios, but that further analysis is needed.
The response is a non-binding policy proposal; no new prohibition or reserve requirement has taken effect. The Commission's consultation closes on September 30. After reviewing the feedback, the Commission will decide whether to submit amendments to MiCA.
items.metanomia_thought: The proposal would increase constraints on the ways stablecoins can provide returns while giving issuers more flexibility in how they manage reserves. It seeks to block routes that provide users with interest-like rewards, while managing reserves according to how quickly funds for redemptions can be made available rather than according to the share held in bank deposits. The approach distinguishes between functions to permit and risks to control as policymakers define the role stablecoins may play in financial markets.

items.title: Circle Launches Bitcoin-Backed USDC Borrowing for Institutions, Connecting to Morpho Lending Markets
items.content:
On September 21 local time, Circle announced a new feature in Circle Mint, its platform for institutional customers, that allows users to borrow USDC from external lending markets against Bitcoin collateral. Eligible institutional customers can deposit Bitcoin, receive cirBTC tokens backed one-to-one by the deposited Bitcoin, and use those tokens as collateral.
Customers supply cirBTC to an external lending market through a wallet they control and borrow USDC on an overcollateralized basis, providing collateral worth more than the loan. The borrowed USDC is credited to the customer's Circle Mint balance, and repayment allows the cirBTC collateral to be released. Users can borrow USDC through Morpho lending markets operating on the Arc and Ethereum blockchains. Circle said it plans to connect other lending services, including Aave. Interest rates, collateral requirements, liquidation thresholds, and available liquidity are set by the lending market selected by the customer and may change. The feature is designed for institutional customers and is not available to customers in New York.
The Bitcoin backing cirBTC is held by Circle National Trust, a federally chartered trust bank. Circle said the Bitcoin is held for the benefit of cirBTC holders, segregated from company assets, and that reserve information is published onchain through Chainlink's proof-of-reserve function. In Arc's official announcement, Circle said lending services are provided by independent third parties and that Circle does not itself originate or underwrite loans or supply the loan funds.
items.metanomia_thought: One way to expand the use of stablecoins is to help companies raise the funds they need in stablecoin form. Circle has brought together Bitcoin custody, issuance of a collateral token, and access to external lending markets so institutions can obtain USDC through its service. The move suggests that a stablecoin issuer is extending its role as a gateway connecting existing customers with financial services.

items.title: Coinbase Opens IPO Subscriptions to U.S. Retail Users, Starting with Oura and Favoring Longer-Term Holders
items.content:
On September 21 local time, U.S. crypto exchange Coinbase announced a feature allowing U.S. retail users to subscribe through its app for shares in initial public offerings at the offering price. The first offering is Oura's IPO taking place this week. Participation requires a securities account with Coinbase Capital Markets and is currently limited to U.S. residents. Before subscribing, every user must complete an eligibility questionnaire to determine whether restrictions imposed by the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority apply.
On the app's IPO page, users submit a Conditional Offer to Buy within the published offering-price range and receive the result after the subscription period closes. Final allocations may be full, partial, or zero, depending on the supply provided by the underwriters and aggregate customer demand. Coinbase said its allocation algorithm favors investors inclined to hold shares for longer periods. Allocated shares may be sold on Coinbase as soon as public trading begins, but a sale within 30 days may restrict the user from participating in IPOs for the following 60 days. Repeated short-term sales may also reduce the size and frequency of future allocations compared with investors who hold for longer.
The securities are offered by FINRA-registered broker-dealer Coinbase Capital Markets acting as the user's agent, while Apex Clearing Corporation handles clearing. Coinbase disclosed that Securities Investor Protection Corporation protection does not apply to digital assets or cash held in Coinbase, Inc. accounts. The company described the feature as another step toward becoming an “Everything Exchange.” The launch announcement did not state the fees or the maximum subscription amount per person.
items.metanomia_thought: Coinbase is adding IPO subscriptions and allocations to listed-stock brokerage, extending a customer relationship that began with crypto trading into securities investing within a single app. For a limited-supply product such as an IPO, the chance to receive an allocation in a future offering can itself influence customer behavior. Making a short-term sale affect future subscriptions and allocations asks customers to weigh an immediate selling decision against their next investment opportunity. By widening access to IPO subscriptions while allocating more opportunity to users inclined to hold longer, Coinbase is taking on both the role of enabling investment access and the role of selecting among customers.

items.title: ECB Launches ‘Pontes’ Tokenized-Asset Settlement Network; Prepares to Invest Own Funds in Tokenized Securities
items.content:
On September 21 local time, the European Central Bank (ECB) announced the launch of Pontes, which settles inter-institutional transactions in tokenized assets using central bank money. The ECB said the same day that it had also begun preparations to invest a small portion of its own funds in tokenized securities.
Tokenization is the issuance or representation of assets such as bonds and funds as digital tokens recorded on distributed ledger technology (DLT). The ECB said public- and private-sector participants in its 2024 trials had indicated that broad use of the technology would require access to central bank money as a risk-free settlement asset. Pontes is a project of the Eurosystem, comprising the ECB and the national central banks of the euro area, and connects market DLT platforms to TARGET services, the euro settlement infrastructure operated by the Eurosystem. It coordinates processing across platforms so that delivery of securities and payment occur together, while final cash settlement is completed in T2, the real-time gross settlement system. Market participants are limited to institutions with access to T2, and operators of DLT platforms seeking a connection must also meet specified eligibility requirements, including authorization and supervision.
According to the ECB, 13 market participants, including Deutsche Bank and the European Investment Bank, and four DLT operators, including Clearstream and SWIAT, have completed onboarding and are ready to use Pontes immediately. Deutsche Bundesbank is also participating as a market participant. Pontes will initially provide core services, with functionality and operating hours to be expanded in stages toward expected full implementation by 2028. Alongside Pontes, the Eurosystem is pursuing the Appia project to develop a blueprint for a DLT-based financial ecosystem by 2028.
The ECB's initial investments will target euro-denominated tokenized securities issued by central, regional, or local governments and agencies in the euro area, as well as European supranational institutions. Payments for purchases are expected to settle through Pontes in central bank money. The ECB said direct investment would let it gain end-to-end experience spanning trade execution, settlement, and system and portfolio management. Its own-funds portfolio is managed separately from monetary-policy assets and generates income used to cover ECB operating expenses other than costs related to supervisory work. After preparations are complete, the Executive Board will decide the detailed operating arrangements and timing of the investment. The announcements did not state whether any transaction occurred on the day Pontes launched, the amount settled, or the amount the ECB will invest.
items.metanomia_thought: As tokenized finance expands, the connection between platforms that record assets and systems that provide final cash settlement becomes increasingly important. Pontes connects market DLT platforms to the existing central-bank settlement network, preserving the role of central bank money in a new trading environment. The ECB's preparations to invest its own funds can be read as an effort to use the new network directly and develop practical experience with trading and settlement.

items.title: Hana Bank Issues $100 Million Digital Bond via Euroclear, Completing Settlement on Issuance Day
items.content:
Hana Bank said it issued a $100 million, five-year foreign-currency digital bond on September 18 through Euroclear's blockchain-based Digital Financial Market Infrastructure (D-FMI). The bank described it as the first digital-bond issuance by a Korean financial institution directly using Euroclear's blockchain infrastructure and the first same-day settlement (T+0) in Korea's foreign-currency bond issuance market.
According to Hana Bank, allocation of the bonds and transfer of funds, processes that typically take three to five business days, were handled on the blockchain and completed on the issuance date. Standard Chartered served as sole arranger, handling the bond's structuring, issuance, and sale to investors. The issuance used documentation from Hana Bank's existing Global Medium Term Note program. The bank said institutional investors could use their existing Euroclear accounts and trading systems without opening separate digital-asset accounts or completing complex additional procedures.
According to Euroclear, D-FMI handles the issuance and distribution of digital securities and settlement at issuance on a blockchain. The bonds are subsequently moved to Euroclear Bank's existing settlement platform, where secondary-market transactions are settled. The same-day settlement in this case was the initial settlement in which investors paid for and received the bonds at issuance. Hana Bank's release did not disclose the issue yield, the composition of investors, or whether the bonds had subsequently traded in the secondary market.
items.metanomia_thought: For digital bonds to become a practical funding instrument, investor access matters alongside settlement speed. This issuance processed the bond's creation and initial settlement on a blockchain while allowing investors to continue using familiar accounts and trading systems. The significance of the case lies in connecting the new technology to the existing market without placing the full burden of adoption on investors.

items.title: U.S. OCC Conditionally Approves Trust Bank Formation or Conversion for Three Crypto Companies
items.content:
On September 18 local time, the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) conditionally approved applications by Agora, Catena Labs, and Bastion to form or convert federally chartered trust banks. Agora and Catena Labs plan to establish new trust banks, while Bastion plans to convert an existing New York state trust company subsidiary into a federally chartered trust bank.
The three companies are pursuing different businesses. Agora, the issuer of the dollar stablecoin AUSD, plans to offer stablecoin issuance and reserve management, custody, payment, settlement, and investment advisory services through the new bank. After it opens, Agora plans to transfer issuance of AUSD from its Bermuda entity to the new bank. Catena Labs, co-founded by Circle co-founder Sean Neville, describes itself as a financial institution for artificial-intelligence agents. Its new bank plans to provide custody and investment management for fiat currency, securities, and crypto assets, as well as foreign-exchange and clearing services. Bastion issues corporate-branded stablecoins and provides other issuers with technology for issuance, burning, and redemption, as well as reserve management; the assets it may custody will be limited to stablecoins.
None of the three banks will be insured by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation. For their first three years of operation, the OCC requires Agora and Catena to maintain at least $10 million in base capital each and Bastion at least $6 million. Separately from capital-related liquidity requirements, each must also hold eligible liquid assets sufficient to cover 180 days of operating expenses in a wind-down during the same period. Activities that do not comply with the GENIUS Act and related regulations when they take effect must be adjusted, discontinued, or disposed of as necessary. Agora and Catena must raise their capital within 12 months of approval and begin operations within 18 months, while Bastion must complete its conversion within six months unless the OCC grants an extension.
There is also disagreement over the permissible scope of the charters. The Independent Community Bankers of America opposed Agora's application, questioning the activities a trust bank may conduct and competitive parity with existing banks. In its decision, the OCC concluded that Agora's proposed activities are permissible trust-company activities or activities incidental to them. The conditional approvals do not mean the three banks have begun operating; each must satisfy the OCC's conditions, complete the formation or conversion process, and receive final authorization to commence business.
items.metanomia_thought: Stablecoin issuance, enterprise infrastructure, and financial services for AI agents are different businesses, yet all three are converging on the same regulatory route of a federal trust bank charter. This can be read as a broader effort by crypto companies to secure an institutional status that allows them to perform financial functions directly. The disagreement between the ICBA and the OCC centers on how far that route may extend the permissible business of a trust bank. Chartering policy—deciding which businesses receive the status of a bank—is therefore also shaping the business structure of the crypto market.

items.title: World Launches ‘World Money,’ Combining Stablecoin Transfers, Trading, and Yield Services
items.content: On September 17 local time, digital identity and crypto-asset project World announced that it had begun rolling out its World Money financial app in more than 150 countries. World, which changed its name from Worldcoin, has brought together stablecoin storage and transfers, trading, and access to asset-management services in the app. The app is provided by Tools for Humanity, co-founded by Sam Altman, and is based on a self-custodial wallet in which users manage their own assets. According to the company, the app supports stablecoin balances linked to eight currencies, including the U.S. dollar. Users can send supported crypto assets abroad using the recipient's World username. In some regions, users can also receive salary or other funds through individual virtual accounts supported by Bridge. In the United States, a top-up feature connected to payments company Stripe lets users pay with Apple Pay and add stablecoins to the app. The company said this process typically takes only a few minutes. The trading menu allows users to buy and sell supported assets through connected exchanges. In the asset-management menu, users can deposit supported assets, including the Worldcoin token WLD and stablecoins, into programs powered by Morpho to earn rewards. Users who have completed World ID verification through an Orb device receive temporarily boosted rewards in some programs. However, available features, assets, and eligibility vary by country, and services provided by external companies are subject to those companies' terms and conditions.
items.metanomia_thought: For stablecoins to function in everyday finance, the process of moving money into a wallet and reusing received funds needs to be convenient. World Money can be read as an effort to reduce that friction by connecting familiar payment methods and multiple financial services in one app. Adding enhanced rewards for users who prove they are human is a choice to use financial-service benefits as an incentive to participate in World ID verification.

items.title: U.S. SEC Grants Tokenized Listed-Stock Trading Venues a Five-Year Conditional Exemption from Exchange Registration
items.content:
On September 17 local time, the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) granted blockchain-based venues trading tokenized U.S. listed stocks a five-year conditional exemption from the securities-exchange registration requirement. A tokenized listed stock represents ownership of an existing share through a token on a blockchain. Venues meeting the specified conditions may operate without registering as securities exchanges through September 17, 2031.
Eligible tokens must carry the same rights as the underlying shares, including dividends and voting rights; synthetic products that merely track share prices are excluded. Even if a venue uses a public blockchain, only authorized participants who have passed identity and sanctions screening may trade. The exemption applies to trading previously issued shares and does not permit a venue to issue new securities.
To trade shares tokenized by a third party unaffiliated with the issuer, a venue must notify the issuer in writing. Trading may begin only after at least 30 days have passed since the issuer received the notice; if the issuer objects in writing during that period, the shares cannot be traded on that venue.
Limits also apply to the number of stocks and trading volume. If a venue exceeds the volume limit for the same stock a second time after an initial breach, it must halt trading in that stock for three months; volume across affiliated venues is combined when calculating the limit. Trading in a tokenized stock must also halt if trading in the underlying stock is halted on its listing exchange. A venue operating under the exemption is neither registered with nor approved by the SEC and must say so in its disclosures.
items.metanomia_thought: The measure opens a route to trading shares on a blockchain while preserving rights attached to the stock, including dividends and votes. Yet a public blockchain does not remove the requirement for authorized participation, and the issuer's objection process and the existing exchange's trading halts still apply. It can be read as an effort to test a new trading service by changing the technology used for share transactions while retaining shareholder rights and market oversight rules.

items.title: S&P Global Agrees to Acquire OpenZeppelin to Strengthen Smart-Contract Risk Assessment
items.content:
On September 17 local time, financial information and credit-ratings company S&P Global announced an agreement to acquire smart-contract security company OpenZeppelin. Founded in 2015, OpenZeppelin audits smart contracts and supports blockchain development, and it provides an open-source contract library reused by many projects. S&P Global said the acquisition would strengthen its ability to assess risks associated with smart contracts and blockchain technology.
According to the company, OpenZeppelin's library has supported more than $37 trillion in cumulative transfers and is used by most of the largest stablecoins and tokenized funds. OpenZeppelin has also completed more than 900 security audit engagements and identified more than 10,000 vulnerabilities before production. These are company-reported cumulative usage and work metrics, not the value of assets owned or managed by OpenZeppelin.
After the acquisition closes, OpenZeppelin is expected to operate as a separate business unit under its existing name. Co-founder and CEO Demian Brener will continue to lead the business and report to Yann Le Pallec, president of S&P Global Ratings. S&P Global had also announced on September 14 that it was leading an extension of digital-asset data company Kaiko's Series B funding round.
The transaction remains subject to closing conditions; ownership had not transferred at the time of the announcement. The parties did not disclose the purchase price or an expected closing date.
items.metanomia_thought: Even when an issuer's credit and reserve assets are sound, confidence in a tokenized financial product can falter if the code executing its transactions fails. The acquisition can be read as a move to treat code verification as an essential capability in assessing financial-product risk. As financial products move onto blockchains, both the objects of assessment and the expertise required of rating providers are changing.

items.title: UK FCA Orders Three London P2P Crypto Premises to Stop Operating Over Suspected Lack of Registration
items.content:
On September 17 local time, the UK's Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) announced that it had issued cease-and-desist letters to three London premises suspected of operating unregistered peer-to-peer (P2P) crypto businesses. The action took place on September 10 with tax authority HMRC and the Metropolitan Police Service. P2P trading is a way for individuals to buy and sell crypto assets directly with one another. According to the FCA, individuals trading on their own behalf do not need to register, but those providing the service as a business in the UK must register under anti-money-laundering rules. The FCA said no P2P crypto business currently operating in the UK is registered.
The authorities carried out the action under the Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds Regulations 2017. The FCA said unregistered P2P businesses could be used to move illicit funds while avoiding controls intended to detect and prevent money laundering. The action followed the FCA's first joint operation in April, when it targeted eight premises with HMRC and the South West Regional Organised Crime Unit. The FCA said evidence collected then is being used for criminal investigations and other enforcement action. It did not disclose any arrests or charges linked to the September operation or name the three premises.
items.metanomia_thought: Exchanging crypto assets directly without a centralized exchange does not remove the UK's anti-money-laundering registration duty when the activity is offered as a business. Given the FCA's distinction that individuals trading on their own behalf need no registration, the target of this action is not P2P trading itself but premises suspected of offering it commercially without registration. The operation shows that the regulatory boundary turns on the nature of the business, not simply on the trading method.

items.title: U.S. House Tax Committee Advances Crypto Bill; Special Rule Covers Gains or Losses on Fee Payments of $10 or Less
items.content:
On September 16 local time, the U.S. House Ways and Means Committee approved the Digital Asset Tax Certainty Act (H.R. 10357) by 38 votes to 5, The Block reported. The bill sets out provisions across seven titles covering taxation of small fees, stablecoin transactions, lending, application of wash-sale rules, mining and staking income, and broker reporting obligations. Chair Jason Smith said the measure was the first tax framework for digital assets after more than a year of bipartisan work.
One key provision would prevent a taxpayer from recognizing a gain or loss on the disposal of a crypto asset used to pay certain small fees. For a network fee paid to validate a transaction, the total paid for that validation must be $10 or less. For brokerage, trading, liquidity-provision, and similar fees, the total fees paid in the relevant transaction must be $10 or less, and the fee must be paid in the same kind of crypto asset as the asset disposed of or acquired in that transaction. This would neither exempt every small purchase of goods from tax nor eliminate blockchain fees themselves.
Traders, brokers, and dealers in crypto assets; businesses that bundle or help validate transactions for others; and people who transferred crypto assets more than 5,000 times in the preceding tax year would generally be excluded from this special rule. Transfers made to pay small fees would not count toward the 5,000-transfer threshold. The bill would apply the fee provision to asset disposals on or after January 1, 2028.
The bill also contains a provision restricting taxpayers' ability to deduct losses. It would extend the wash-sale rule that applies to stocks and securities to traded digital assets, while generally excluding qualified dollar stablecoins. If a taxpayer sells an asset at a loss and acquires a substantially identical asset within 30 days before or after the sale, the loss could not be deducted immediately and would instead be reflected in the replacement asset's basis. Assets received through validation activities such as mining or staking, and regular acquisitions included in ordinary income, would not count as reacquisitions for this purpose. The bill sets September 15, 2026, as the starting date for disposals subject to this provision, earlier than the start date proposed for the fee rule.
The bill would also classify income from validation activities, including mining and staking, as ordinary income. According to The Block, Representative Steven Horsford, who worked on the bill, said it still did not resolve when mining and staking income should be recognized. Another provision would prevent a trustee from losing a trust's tax status solely because the trustee has authority to stake the crypto assets it holds. That special treatment would not apply if the trustee conducts digital-asset transaction validation as a business.
The committee vote is a step in the House legislative process, not the enactment of the proposed tax rules; further steps, including consideration by the full House, remain. The Block reported that attention would next turn to the Senate Finance Committee.
items.metanomia_thought: Making crypto assets easier to use for payments depends on simpler tax treatment as well as network performance. If every small fee paid with a crypto asset requires a gain-or-loss calculation on disposal, a technically simple transaction remains cumbersome for the user. The bill takes an approach that separates fee payments from the realization of investment losses, applying different tax rules to different uses of crypto assets. Both the businesses building payment services and the lawmakers deciding which transactions receive lighter tax treatment shape how practical those assets are to use.

items.title: Deutsche Bank Plans Crypto Custody for European Institutions and Businesses This Year, Subject to Regulatory Steps
items.content:
On September 16 local time, Deutsche Bank announced plans to launch a crypto-asset custody service for European institutions and businesses this year. The first customers' use of the service is conditional on completion of the relevant regulatory steps. Under the custody service, the bank would manage wallets and private keys on customers' behalf to hold assets and enable transfers to third parties. The bank said this would reduce customers' burden of building and maintaining their own custody infrastructure. Initial supported assets are expected to include bitcoin, ether, and the stablecoins USDC, EURC, and EURAU. EURAU is a euro stablecoin issued by AllUnity, a joint venture involving Deutsche Bank's asset-management affiliate DWS. Target customers include businesses using the bank's corporate-banking and investment-banking divisions, asset managers, hedge funds, custodians, brokers, and government entities; access will be subject to the bank's criteria, due-diligence requirements, and risk appetite. The bank said its security design includes secure key generation, hardware-based protection of private keys, segregation of duties, multiple approvals, separate warm and cold storage, redundant technology, and controlled backup and recovery procedures.
Gerald Podobnik, co-head of corporate banking, said crypto assets were a complement rather than a replacement for the traditional financial system, offering a new route that could coexist with established market infrastructure while benefiting from the trust and safeguards provided by a regulated financial institution. The bank plans to expand the range of supported assets or handle tokenized financial products depending on customer demand, product approvals, risk management, and regulatory procedures. It said the launch timing, regions, supported assets, and scope could change because of regulatory requirements or internal approvals. It also stated that crypto assets held in custody do not receive the same deposit protection as eligible bank deposits.
items.metanomia_thought: The announcement points to a continued move by traditional banks to bring crypto assets into their existing financial services. Deutsche Bank's preparations for custody aimed at corporate and investment-banking customers suggest it sees crypto assets as a category of client property requiring ongoing management. As such services develop, institutions and businesses may have more options to hold and manage crypto assets through banks they already work with. South Korea also needs to clarify which crypto-asset activities traditional financial institutions may undertake and where their responsibilities lie, while establishing a predictable regulatory framework.

items.title: Ondo Subsidiary Joins DTCC's Fund/SERV Network, Standardizing Connections to Existing Fund Distributors
items.content:
On September 16 local time, the Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC) and Ondo Finance announced that Ondo subsidiary Oasis Pro Markets had become a member of Fund/SERV. Ondo is a technology company that turns financial assets into tokens on a blockchain. Oasis Pro Markets, the entity that joined the network, is a broker-dealer registered with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and an alternative trading system (ATS) operator; it acts as a distributor of tokenized investment products. Fund/SERV is established financial-market infrastructure that electronically processes and settles transactions between fund companies and distributors. The companies described this as the first participation by a tokenization platform in Fund/SERV.
Instead of building a separate connection for every fund, Oasis Pro Markets can use one standardized connection to conduct transaction-related business with fund companies, wealth-management platforms, and service providers. The connection supports the exchange of account-level information, trade confirmations, reconciliation between parties' books, distribution payments, and information needed for tax and regulatory reporting. According to DTCC, Fund/SERV processes more than 85% of U.S. mutual-fund transaction activity. Ondo said participation in the network lays the groundwork for connecting tokenized funds to existing fund-distribution channels.
The joint announcement did not identify a particular Ondo product that had begun trading through Fund/SERV or give a date for a first trade. What has taken place is a broker-dealer's admission to a processing network, which is distinct from the launch of sales of any individual tokenized fund or regulatory approval of a product.
items.metanomia_thought: For tokenized funds to reach existing distribution channels, firms must be able to exchange orders, account data, and settlement information as well as put assets into token form. A single standardized connection reduces the need to build separate links for each fund and helps connect tokenized products with the systems existing distributors already use. This membership shows that tokenized finance can reach users not only by replacing established financial networks, but also by using their distribution and settlement infrastructure.

items.title: Circle Launches Arc Mainnet, Linking Payments, Finance and AI Wallets with USDC Fees
items.content:
On September 16 local time, Circle announced the launch of the public mainnet of Arc, a blockchain designed for payments, financial transactions, and the economic activity of artificial intelligence (AI) agents. The company said more than 100 applications and more than 100 institutions and ecosystem participants were involved on the first day. Arc is designed to let businesses and developers build connected payment, foreign-exchange, and lending services on the same network. Transaction fees are paid in the dollar stablecoin USDC, so users do not need to hold a separate, volatile token for fees, according to Circle. The company said transactions on the network reach finality in less than one second. Arc is also compatible with existing Ethereum development tools and smart contracts.
Circle said Circle StableFX, which supports round-the-clock foreign-exchange trading between stablecoins, is live on Arc. The company identified more than 20 stablecoins for launch or integration. It also said Circle Payments Network, which connects payment providers to Arc's payment layer and StableFX, has been integrated. Lending markets from Aave and Morpho and trading services including Uniswap can be used in the same environment, the company said. Arc Portal lets users create and fund wallets for themselves and AI agents. Users can set spending limits and permissions for agent wallets before assigning them financial tasks. Circle Agent Stack is a set of tools that supports these controlled wallets and USDC nanopayments of less than one cent.
Permissioned validators handle transaction validation. Circle said participation by its initial validator group, which includes BlackRock, the Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC), and Visa alongside Circle, is expected to be phased in. A privacy feature that would let businesses selectively conceal transaction information or balances is still being developed for network-wide availability.
Circle said it technically created an initial supply of 10 billion ARC tokens in the United States this week, and claimed to be the first publicly listed company to create a network token for a new layer-1 blockchain. It stressed that this creation is a technical milestone in considering a transition to proof of stake in 2027, not a commitment to a public launch of ARC. Network fees will continue to be paid in USDC. According to Arc's disclosures, the network is offered by Arc Network Services LLC and operated by permissioned validators. The disclosures also say that the Arc network has not been reviewed or approved by regulators and that there is no recourse for transaction errors or losses.
items.metanomia_thought: When businesses adopt a blockchain, they need to manage fees, funds, and AI spending authority as well as transaction speed. Connecting payments, foreign exchange, and lending in one environment could make it easier to build services that put received funds to work in other financial activities. Spending limits and permissions on AI wallets combine the ability for software to send money with a person's ability to define how that money may be used. The practical change in this launch is the opening of an execution environment in which people and software can use the same funds and financial tools.

items.title: U.S. Senate Fails to Advance CLARITY Act as 49 Votes in Favor Fall Short of 60-Vote Threshold
items.content:
On September 15, local time, a procedural vote in the U.S. Senate to advance consideration of the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act (CLARITY Act) failed. The bill would define the supervisory roles of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), as well as trading rules, in cryptoasset markets. According to the official roll call, the vote was 49 in favor, 50 against, and one not voting, short of the 60 votes required. This was not a vote on final passage of the bill. It was a vote on whether to end debate on the motion to proceed to the bill and move to the next stage. Some Republicans also voted no, but according to the Senate's record of proceedings, Thom Tillis cast his vote against it so that he could file a motion to reconsider. Immediately after the result was announced, Tillis filed a motion to reconsider the outcome of the procedural vote.
The Block reported that President Donald Trump's cryptoasset businesses and conflicts of interest involving public officials were key points of contention. According to The Block, Democratic Senator Mark Warner said he opposed advancing consideration of the bill because conflicts of interest surrounding the president's cryptoasset businesses remained unresolved. The outcome blocked further progress on the bill, but did not mean that it had been definitively rejected. The Block reported that another procedural vote could be held if Senate floor time became available.
items.metanomia_thought: In the process of establishing rules for cryptoasset businesses, both market oversight and conflicts of interest involving public officials are becoming points on which agreement must be reached. Even when votes in favor are secured, some stages, such as this procedural vote, require a separate voting threshold to be met. Support for a bill therefore does not necessarily translate into actual legislative progress. This vote does not put new rules into effect; it shows that the political agreement needed to move deliberations forward has yet to be secured.

items.title: Nasdaq Verafin and Stablecore Combine Monitoring of Bank Transactions and Crypto Asset Flows in Pilot at Selected Institutions
items.content: On September 15, local time, Nasdaq Verafin and Stablecore announced a partnership to detect financial crime by examining bank transactions and digital asset transactions together. Verafin helps financial institutions detect fraud and money laundering, while Stablecore connects stablecoins, tokenized deposits, and other digital assets to the existing systems of banks and credit unions. The companies explained that financial institutions may miss suspicious flows of funds between fiat currencies and digital assets if they lack sufficient visibility into blockchain transactions. Stablecore provides information on digital asset holdings and transactions, while banks supply the necessary data from their core banking systems, which manage customer and account information. Verafin combines information from both systems into a single record for each customer for use in investigations and risk assessments. According to the announcement, Stablecore itself does not hold personally identifiable information. The service is currently being piloted at selected institutions, including Amarillo National Bank. The companies plan to expand the service to their joint customers between the fourth quarter of 2026 and the first quarter of 2027. They said a feature that checks in real time whether the recipient of a digital asset transfer is subject to sanctions will be added after the initial integration.
items.metanomia_thought: Bringing stablecoins into banking requires more than the ability to transfer money. It also requires a system that can put those transactions in the context of existing customer information. When bank customers move money between deposits and digital assets, examining both sets of records together may help identify flows of funds that could easily be missed when each is examined on its own.

This investment provides capital to expand that connecting infrastructure. The amount raised does not, by itself, indicate the scale of use or the cost savings achieved.

items.title: U.S. Prosecutors Charge Two Former Robinhood Engineers with Fraud, Alleging Perpetual Futures Trades Using Nonpublic Listing Information
items.content:
On September 15, local time, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York released two criminal complaints against Hefu Chai and Huaisong Xiang, who had worked as engineers at financial services company Robinhood. Prosecutors alleged that the two used nonpublic information about Robinhood Crypto's listing plans and timing, obtained through their work between 2025 and 2026, for personal trading. According to the allegations, they traded perpetual futures contracts on tokens scheduled to be listed, using Hyperliquid, which describes itself as a decentralized exchange. Perpetual futures are derivatives with no expiration date whose gains and losses depend on changes in the price of the underlying asset, rather than direct purchases of that asset.
According to the complaints, listing information was shared in an internal chat room accessible only to designated employees. The company's insider trading policy prohibited those employees from making related trades on Robinhood or other platforms before listing announcements and for 24 hours afterward. The complaint against Xiang described an instance in March 2025 in which, after receiving listing information about POPCAT, he took a position betting on a price increase and closed it at a profit after actual trading had begun on Robinhood but before the public announcement.
Prosecutors alleged that each man earned more than $50,000 through such trades. Each was charged with one count of commodities fraud and one count of wire fraud. Prosecutors said that company insiders who improperly use nonpublic information to trade cannot avoid the application of securities and commodities laws even if the instruments traded are perpetual futures or tokenized securities. They explicitly stated that the claims in the complaints are allegations only and that both men are presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty in court. According to The Block, Robinhood said it immediately conducted an internal investigation into the matter, reported it to law enforcement and regulators, and would continue to cooperate with the investigation.
items.metanomia_thought: The case illustrates how the value of listing information held by one company can translate into trading profits in derivatives markets outside that company. The conduct described by prosecutors involves employees with access to inside information betting on price movements on another platform, making it difficult to explain the full chain of events from the company's own trading records alone. The focus of the case is less on the fact that trading took place on a blockchain than on whether confidential information obtained through work was used for personal trading, and those allegations remain to be proven in criminal proceedings.

items.title: Attorneys General from 17 U.S. States and Washington, D.C. Oppose CLARITY Act, Seek to Preserve State Fraud Enforcement and Registration Powers
items.content:
On September 14 local time, New York Attorney General Letitia James released a joint letter opposing the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act, or CLARITY Act, and calling for states to retain their authority to combat crypto asset fraud. A total of 18 attorneys general, representing 17 states including New York and Washington, D.C., joined the letter. They asked Senate Banking Committee Chair Tim Scott and Ranking Democrat Elizabeth Warren to oppose the current bill until state authority is adequately preserved. The signatories emphasized that state securities licensing and registration regimes are investor protection tools that support examinations, investigations, and fraud enforcement. Although the bill retains some fraud enforcement powers, they also raised concerns that ambiguous or restrictive wording could lead to jurisdictional disputes and litigation delays.
In particular, they expressed concern that the bill would add a new category of "qualified transaction" to the Securities Act of 1933 that would be exempt from state registration requirements and allow the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, or SEC, to define its scope broadly. They argued that the effects could extend beyond crypto assets to state oversight of traditional securities markets. They therefore called for preserving state enforcement authority over securities regardless of whether they are tokenized, maintaining federal-state cooperation, explicitly recognizing the states' role in crypto asset oversight in the law, preserving platform registration regimes, and clarifying ambiguous language. According to The Block, an amendment released on September 13 included a provision allowing state attorneys general to participate in enforcing crypto asset conflict-of-interest rules for public officials. The Senate is scheduled to hold a procedural vote on September 15 to decide whether to advance consideration of the bill, The Block reported.
items.metanomia_thought: As nationwide rules for crypto assets are developed, it is also important to determine how to preserve the role of state governments that have investigated local reports of harm and supervised trading firms. Adding authority to investigate conflicts of interest involving public officials and preserving registration and fraud enforcement powers over trading platforms are separate issues. This opposition can be read as a request to state clearly in the bill the grounds on which states will still be able to investigate and hold parties accountable after federal rules are established.

items.content:
On September 14 local time, financial information company S&P Global announced that it had led an additional investment in crypto asset data company Kaiko. The investment was made through S&P Global Ventures, S&P Global's venture investment arm. Kaiko provides banks, asset managers, and other institutions with crypto asset trading prices, market analytics, and indices. According to Kaiko, the investment increased the cumulative amount raised in its Series B round to $110 million. The size of this additional investment and S&P Global's individual investment were not disclosed in the companies' announcements. BNP Paribas, Nasdaq Ventures, Coinbase Ventures, and others also participated.
Kaiko said it currently handles data from more than 150 exchanges and protocols. The company explained that if financial products are to trade on blockchains 24 hours a day, the supporting market data must also be available without interruption. Kaiko's data infrastructure sends market information to smart contracts and converts financial transactions conducted on blockchains into standardized data that can be used in traditional systems. The company plans to use the funding to strengthen its existing data business and expand infrastructure for tokenized markets. Participating institutions will also join an industry working group chaired by Kaiko to discuss the direction of the data and infrastructure needed to operate tokenized products in practice. S&P Global said the two companies had launched a suite of co-branded crypto asset indices in early September and that this investment expands their existing partnership.
items.metanomia_thought: For financial institutions to operate tokenized products, they need not only to place assets on a blockchain but also to have data for checking prices and calculating risk. This investment and participation in the working group can be read as a move by financial institutions to become more directly involved in supplying and designing the data they need. Tokenized products can be connected to routine financial operations only when market data is delivered to smart contracts and onchain transactions are organized so that existing systems can understand them.

items.title: WTO Analyzes Stablecoin Use in Trade, Says Foreign Exchange Costs and Links to Existing Financial Networks Will Determine Impact
items.content:
On September 14 local time, the World Trade Organization, or WTO, Secretariat released a report analyzing the potential uses and challenges of stablecoins in international trade at the first World Trade and Technology Day event. The report explained that cross-border payments passing through multiple banks and foreign exchange stages are slow and expensive, with these burdens falling particularly heavily on small and medium-sized enterprises and businesses in developing countries. Stablecoins are privately issued digital assets designed to track the value of a reference asset such as the U.S. dollar. Citing an early-2025 estimate published by McKinsey, the report said stablecoins accounted for about 3% of global cross-border payment value and were not being used at scale in trade finance beyond some pilot projects. The report found that sending funds through stablecoins without time-zone constraints could shorten processing times in some payment corridors and reduce intermediary costs. However, it noted that actual costs must include not only blockchain transaction fees but also the cost of acquiring stablecoins, regulatory compliance costs, and foreign exchange costs when conversion into local currency is required. A study cited by the report found that the total cost of some international remittance corridors using a single stablecoin ranged from 0.3% to nearly 9% of the amount sent, with costs arising mainly at the stages where fiat currency and stablecoins are exchanged. Know-your-customer, anti-money laundering, and sanctions screening procedures also remain necessary.
The report analyzed that because stablecoins do not themselves provide loans, guarantees, or insurance, their benefits may currently be more direct for cross-border payments for digital services than for goods trade, which requires credit provision. It added, however, that assessments of their role in trade finance could change as tokenization, legal frameworks, and market infrastructure develop. It also said that while stablecoins could improve access to international payments for businesses in developing countries, widespread use of stablecoins based on foreign currencies could displace domestic currencies, weaken the effectiveness of monetary policy, and increase dependence on foreign private issuers. The report concluded that broader use would require clear redemption rights and reserve asset management standards, as well as links among banking systems, corporate treasury management, and electronic trade documents. The report was prepared under the responsibility of the WTO Secretariat and does not necessarily reflect the positions of WTO members, nor is it intended to provide an authoritative or legal interpretation of WTO agreements.
items.metanomia_thought: The report points out that stablecoins do not themselves provide the credit needed for trade and that foreign exchange costs can limit payment efficiency. However, if stablecoins received as trade payments can be used directly for the next transaction or for local payments, the cost of converting them into fiat currency each time could be reduced. If this is combined with a structure that tokenizes payment claims contained in invoices and connects them to investor funds, stablecoins could also be used as a means of linking corporate financing and repayment. If this trend spreads, businesses could move beyond holding stablecoin receipts and reusing them for subsequent transactions to participate in a financial environment where they can also raise needed funds through tokenized assets.

items.title: UK FCA Seeks Views on Gold Tokenization Regulation, Considers Exempting Some Products from Fund Rules
items.content:
On September 14 local time, the UK's Financial Conduct Authority, or FCA, opened a consultation on the opportunities and risks of creating tokens representing gold for trading or use as collateral in wholesale markets, as well as the regulation that would be required. Gold tokenization is a method of representing ownership of physical gold held in custody with digital tokens and transferring that ownership electronically. Noting that London's over-the-counter spot gold market is the world's largest, the FCA said this approach could make gold easier to transfer and use as collateral in transactions between financial institutions, provided there is legal certainty and risk control. The review covers only products that grant ownership of physical gold, allow the gold held in custody to be verified, and have reliable redemption procedures.
A key issue is that uncertainty over whether some gold tokens qualify as collective investment schemes, or CISs, or alternative investment funds, or AIFs, could restrict investors from holding them or firms from selling them. Products that provide direct ownership of specific gold bars and do not pool them for collective management are likely to fall outside fund regulation, but fund rules could apply where multiple people share interests in a single gold bar and it is jointly managed or disposed of. The FCA is considering explaining existing rules more clearly, creating a "qualifying gold token" classification, and working with the Treasury to exempt certain gold token products or related market infrastructure from these rules. However, an exemption is only one of several options under consideration, and consideration of it is itself subject to the Treasury's discretion, so no decision has been made on whether it will be implemented. The FCA said a broader exemption should be limited to products that could be protected more effectively under a separate regulatory framework, which should cover ownership, custody of physical gold, redemption, independent verification, and investor protection in the event of insolvency. Responses are due by October 23, and the FCA plans to use the evidence submitted to determine whether guidance or a separate regulatory framework is needed.
items.metanomia_thought: Holders of tokenized gold could gain more ways to use it as collateral in financial transactions without selling the gold. However, that benefit depends on the transfer of a token resulting in the transfer of rights to the physical gold and on holders being able to redeem the gold when needed. This discussion shows that financial market use will depend not only on the technology used to represent gold as tokens but also on the rights and protections attached to those tokens.

items.title: Blockstream Demands Return of Remaining Approximately 598.5 BTC from Liquid Attacker, Rejects '10% Bounty' Payment
items.content:
On September 11 Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), Blockstream said it would not pay compensation to recover approximately 598.5 BTC that the Liquid Network attacker had not returned. The announcement followed a September 6 incident in which actual bitcoin was withdrawn after approximately 3,998.5 unbacked L-BTC had been created on Liquid.
L-BTC is an asset designed to correspond one-to-one with bitcoin held by the Liquid federation. Security firm CertiK analyzed that an error in Liquid's validation software caused the inspection result for a valid transaction to be incorrectly applied to other transactions. The attacker exploited this flaw to create L-BTC without depositing actual bitcoin and then received approximately 4,000 BTC through SideSwap, a federation member that exchanges L-BTC for bitcoin. According to the federation's incident report, the reserve of approximately 4,205 BTC fell to 197 BTC when this withdrawal was combined with other withdrawals processed before operations were suspended. The federation said no private keys were exposed in the process. SideSwap acknowledged in its own statement that it kept the keys used to approve withdrawals on an internet-connected server, automatically delivered bitcoin provided by the federation to users, and imposed no limits on the amount or frequency of withdrawals.
The attacker returned 3,400 BTC to a federation wallet on September 7 but kept approximately 598.5 BTC. In a message included in a Bitcoin transaction on September 9, the attacker demanded that Blockstream pay a 10% bug bounty from its own funds and wrote that refusal would cause L-BTC holders to suffer a 15% loss. Blockstream characterized taking assets without authorization and delaying their return as theft, and said Bitcoin does not impose a haircut on user assets to pay compensation. It also said that if the remaining bitcoin is not returned, it plans to trace the flow of funds with law enforcement agencies, exchanges, service providers, and forensic experts.
Liquid released Elements v23.3.4, which fixed the error, on September 9 and then resumed block production and normal transactions in sequence on September 10. However, the peg-out function that converts L-BTC into bitcoin remains suspended until the reserve has been restored.
items.metanomia_thought: Adding a separate payment and settlement layer on top of Bitcoin can expand speed and functionality, but users must also trust that the layer properly validates assets and releases bitcoin securely. In this incident, actual bitcoin was withdrawn even though no private keys were exposed because an error that accepted unbacked L-BTC as a valid asset coincided with an operating model that imposed no limits on withdrawal size or frequency. Fixing the code error and resuming transactions does not by itself restore redemption capacity. Users will be able to redeem L-BTC for bitcoin only after the reserve is restored and peg-outs resume.

items.title: MoneyGram launches its first stablecoin-backed Visa card in Colombia, enabling payments from app balances and cash pickup at locations
items.content:
On September 10, local time, international money transfer company MoneyGram launched the MoneyGram Card, a stablecoin-backed Visa card, in Colombia. According to The Block, this is MoneyGram's first stablecoin-backed card. The digital card allows users to hold a balance tied to the value of the dollar in the MoneyGram app and use it for everyday payments. Eligible users in Colombia can apply for the card in the MoneyGram app and activate it after completing the required identity verification. Adding the card to Apple Wallet or Google Wallet allows them to pay by phone at Visa merchants or use it for online purchases. When they need cash, they can send the balance in the MoneyGram app to themselves and collect it in local currency at a nearby MoneyGram location. According to the fee schedule linked on the product page, the digital card has no issuance fee, monthly or annual fee, or purchase fee at launch, but a $1 monthly inactivity fee applies after three consecutive months without card activity.
Rain provides the underlying card technology, while Crossmint provides wallet functionality, and the service uses the Stellar network. According to The Block, a company spokesperson said the card supports USDC at launch and that MoneyGram plans to add support soon for MGUSD, its own dollar stablecoin introduced in June. Colombia is currently the only launch market, but MoneyGram said it plans to expand to other markets over the coming months. MoneyGram plans to add a physical card in the latter part of 2026, enabling ATM cash withdrawals and payments at stores where using a digital card is difficult. The cash pickup currently available at MoneyGram locations works by sending an app balance to oneself and collecting it in local currency.
items.metanomia_thought: Users now have more options: they can hold received funds as a dollar-value balance or spend them with a card, rather than simply collecting the money in cash. Connecting Visa merchants with MoneyGram's cash pickup locations lets users spend their money without requiring the other party to use a separate stablecoin wallet. This launch shows how stablecoin use can expand through connections to existing card and cash networks, rather than through the creation of an entirely separate payment network.

items.title: Coinbase and Moov to connect community banks and credit unions to stablecoin payments, integrating custody and settlement into existing financial networks
items.content:
On September 10, local time, Coinbase announced a partnership with payments infrastructure company Moov to enable U.S. community banks and credit unions to offer stablecoin payments, settlement, and asset custody within their existing systems. Moov provides financial institutions with infrastructure for merchant card payment processing, card issuing, and connections to real-time payment networks. Its existing financial institution customers number more than 1,000 across the United States. The partnership will integrate custodial wallet accounts and payment application programming interfaces (APIs) from the Coinbase Developer Platform (CDP) into Moov's existing payments platform. Coinbase will provide the regulated digital asset infrastructure required for asset custody and stablecoin transfers, while Moov will connect it to the payment systems that financial institutions and their customers already use. The proposed use cases include consumer stablecoin payments, merchant payment acceptance and settlement, and disbursements to businesses and merchants.
Coinbase said local financial institutions can add these capabilities to their existing services without building a separate crypto technology stack from scratch. Moov co-founder and CEO Wade Arnold explained the background to the partnership: business customers of local financial institutions are being asked to accept stablecoin payments, but currently have to use services outside their primary financial institution to do so. Arnold identified uninterrupted real-time money movement, including on weekends and holidays, as the next step. The announcement did not specify when services would begin at individual financial institutions or identify institutions that had actually adopted them.
items.metanomia_thought: The significance of this partnership lies in its attempt to give local financial institutions a way to offer stablecoin payments within existing financial relationships, without sending customers to external crypto services. Connecting Coinbase's custody and payment capabilities to Moov's payment infrastructure can lower the adoption burden for smaller financial institutions, which would otherwise have to build a separate technology stack themselves. However, even if the customer relationship remains with the local financial institution, the storage and movement of funds rely on Coinbase's custodial accounts and APIs. The institution a user deals with and the underlying infrastructure that actually handles the assets are therefore distinct.

items.title: ESMA highlights EU authorization gaps and investor risks in prediction markets, distinguishing financial, crypto-asset, and gambling rules by contract characteristics
items.content:
On September 10, local time, the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) highlighted gaps in European Union (EU) authorization and investor protection issues in prediction markets in its second risk monitoring report of 2026. Prediction markets allow people to buy and sell contracts whose payouts depend on the outcomes of future events, such as elections. Discussing major platforms outside the EU, including Polymarket and Kalshi, the report explained that marketing or selling event contracts in the EU generally requires EU authorization. It described Kalshi as regulated by the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) as a designated contract market, while characterizing Polymarket as a partially decentralized platform that combines on-chain trading and settlement with centralized market operations. The report noted that the largest prediction market platforms, including these two, currently lack EU authorization. Although Polymarket and Kalshi block orders from users in some EU countries, they do not restrict users in every member state. The report also assessed the effectiveness of geographic restrictions as uncertain, given that access can be circumvented using a virtual private network (VPN).
The report considered the applicable rules to depend on the underlying subject and structure of an event contract. The Markets in Financial Instruments Directive (MiFID II) may apply if the contract qualifies as a financial instrument, the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA) may apply if it is a crypto-asset based on distributed ledger technology but not a financial instrument, and national gambling rules may apply if it has the characteristics of gambling. The report explained that event contracts qualifying as financial instruments are generally classified as derivatives and fall under national product intervention measures concerning binary options, under which marketing, distribution, and sale to retail investors are prohibited. In addition to insider trading and market manipulation, ESMA identified risks arising from ambiguous definitions and determinations of event outcomes, errors or manipulation in external data, opaque platform resolution procedures, and delayed or failed payouts and settlement. The report acknowledged that prediction market prices may have informational and analytical value by showing real-time updates to expectations about future events. However, it assessed platforms without EU authorization as offering retail investors a speculative gambling environment without the safeguards available for regulated financial products. It concluded that continued monitoring is necessary in light of market developments and emerging risks, even though prediction markets remain limited in size within the EU. It did not announce new regulatory measures.
items.metanomia_thought: Even services that allow bets on the same event may require different authorizations depending on how their contracts are designed and to whom they are sold. The fact that trading takes place on a blockchain does not remove financial instrument regulation or place every contract under crypto-asset rules. This report shows that prediction markets' ability to aggregate information and the presence of safeguards to protect users are separate questions.
